case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory of fraud—which criminalizes the deprivation of complete and accurate information bearing on a person's economic decision—constitutes a valid basis for property fraud liability under the federal wire fraud statute.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1343 (Federal Wire Fraud Statute), with secondary reference to 18 U.S.C. § 1346 (Honest Services Fraud Statute) in related companion cases
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Louis Ciminelli argues that the Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory impermissibly extends federal fraud law beyond the protection of traditional, tangible property rights by treating the deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information' necessary for 'discretionary economic decisions' as a cognizable property interest. Ciminelli contends this theory creates an unconstitutionally vague and overbroad all-purpose federal fraud mechanism that criminalizes conduct far removed from conventional property deprivation, violating the principle that federal fraud statutes protect only traditional property rights and not ethereal or intangible informational interests.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States, as respondent, defends the Second Circuit's right-to-control theory by arguing that the deprivation of economically valuable information that a victim needs to make informed financial decisions constitutes a sufficient property interest under the wire fraud statute, and that the jury instructions in this case correctly reflected a valid theory of money or property fraud. The government maintains that protecting victims' ability to make fully informed economic decisions falls within the legitimate scope of federal fraud statutes.
key_precedents: United States v. Binday, 804 F.3d 558 (2d Cir. 2015) — established the right-to-control theory defining deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information' as property fraud
Carpenter v. United States, 484 U.S. 19 (1987) — foundational case recognizing confidential business information as property under fraud statutes
McNally v. United States, 483 U.S. 350 (1987) — Supreme Court limited mail fraud to protection of property rights, rejecting intangible rights theory
Cleveland v. United States, 531 U.S. 12 (2000) — Supreme Court narrowed the definition of 'property' under federal fraud statutes
Skilling v. United States, 561 U.S. 358 (2010) — Supreme Court limited honest services fraud to bribery and kickback schemes
Kelly v. United States, 590 U.S. 391 (2020) — Supreme Court reaffirmed that federal fraud statutes require deprivation of traditional property rights
United States v. Percoco, No. 21-1158 — companion case involving honest services fraud under § 1346
United States v. Kaloyeros, No. 21-1169 — companion case consolidated for certiorari review
United States v. Aiello and Gerardi, No. 21-1161 — companion case with co-defendants supporting petitioner's position

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of unanimity, and I find myself in agreement with the core reasoning shared across the ideological spectrum. Justice Kagan's observation that treating 'potentially valuable economic information' as property 'effectively resurrects the intangible-rights theory that McNally squarely rejected' is particularly well-stated and aligns with my minimalist instinct to resolve this case on the narrowest available ground. Justice Jackson's point about fair notice and the burden that vague, expansive criminal theories place on under-resourced defendants reinforces the institutional legitimacy concerns that animate my approach. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward a narrow holding—one that invalidates the right-to-control theory as applied to informational interests without necessarily foreclosing every conceivable application of the theory, thereby preserving the Court's institutional credibility and avoiding unnecessary dicta that could create new uncertainties in adjacent areas of fraud law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: My colleagues have presented a remarkably unified front, and I find their collective reasoning persuasive precisely because it converges on the same textual and historical foundation that anchors my own analysis. Justice Gorsuch's observation about Congress's targeted response in enacting § 1346 is particularly telling from an originalist perspective: when Congress wished to extend fraud liability to an intangible right after McNally, it did so explicitly and narrowly, which confirms that § 1343's 'money or property' language carries its traditional common law meaning and does not silently encompass informational interests. Justice Barrett's methodological point about consistency is equally compelling—the original public meaning of 'property' at the time of § 1343's 1952 enactment simply did not encompass a freestanding right to receive complete and accurate information bearing on economic decisions, and no amount of prosecutorial creativity can alter that historical fact. The strongest argument for the respondent—that Carpenter v. United States recognized confidential business information as property—is distinguishable because Carpenter involved a defendant's own property interest in information, not a victim's abstract right to receive information necessary for decision-making, a distinction that Kelly v. United States itself reinforces by requiring that the object of the scheme be traditional property.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The unanimity of my colleagues across the ideological spectrum—from Justice Thomas's originalist analysis to Justice Sotomayor's pragmatic concern for defendants' fair notice—powerfully confirms that the Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory cannot survive scrutiny under any serious judicial methodology. Justice Gorsuch makes the most compelling structural point: Congress's deliberate enactment of § 1346 to cover 'honest services' as a specific, narrow intangible right demonstrates that when Congress wants to extend wire fraud liability beyond traditional property, it knows how to do so explicitly—and its silence regarding informational interests in economic decision-making is therefore dispositive. Justice Barrett's methodological consistency argument is equally persuasive: permitting the right-to-control theory after McNally, Cleveland, and Kelly would effectively nullify three decades of careful line-drawing by this Court and invite prosecutors to resurrect whatever expansive theory this Court most recently rejected. The strongest argument for the respondent—that sophisticated commercial fraud causing real economic harm should be federally cognizable—fails because it is a policy argument properly addressed to Congress, not a textual or doctrinal basis for stretching 'property' beyond its historically grounded meaning.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I find myself in rare but genuine agreement with my conservative colleagues across the board. Justice Jackson's point about the rule of lenity and fair notice resonates deeply with my own concerns about how vague criminal statutes harm vulnerable defendants—the very people I most worry about. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be that sophisticated fraudsters who deprive victims of economically valuable information cause real harm that deserves federal prosecution, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, the proper response to that concern is for Congress to speak clearly, as it did when enacting § 1346 for honest services fraud. The 'right to control' theory's boundlessness is precisely what troubles me most: a standard criminalizing deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information bearing on discretionary decisions' provides no principled limiting principle and would expose ordinary commercial conduct to federal prosecution, which ultimately harms less sophisticated defendants who cannot predict what the government will charge.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling about the strength of the textual case here. Justice Jackson's point about fair notice and the rule of lenity resonates particularly with my pragmatic approach—a criminal statute that cannot tell ordinary actors what conduct is prohibited fails the most basic function of law, and the 'right to control' theory's amorphous standard of 'potentially valuable economic information bearing on discretionary decisions' provides no workable limiting principle. Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies the structural-textual signal in Congress's enactment of § 1346: when Congress wanted to extend fraud liability to an intangible right, it did so explicitly and narrowly, which confirms that the baseline term 'property' in § 1343 does not silently encompass such interests. The strongest argument for the respondent—that Carpenter v. United States recognized confidential business information as property, suggesting intangible interests can qualify—does not save the right-to-control theory, because Carpenter involved a recognized, discrete property interest in specific information, not the diffuse 'right to make fully informed decisions,' and that distinction is precisely what Kelly v. United States reinforces when it requires that the object of the fraud be property in the defendant's hands.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling—when textualists and pragmatists alike converge on the same result, the legal case is strong. Justice Thomas correctly identifies that the original public meaning of 'property' at the time of § 1343's enactment did not encompass a freestanding informational interest in making fully informed economic decisions, and Justice Jackson's point about fair notice and the rule of lenity resonates with my own concern that criminal statutes must give defendants clear warning of what conduct is prohibited. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be that Carpenter v. United States recognized confidential business information as property, suggesting that informational interests can qualify—but Carpenter involved a defendant's own proprietary information that was taken and converted, not a victim's abstract right to receive complete information before making a discretionary decision, which is a categorically different and far more attenuated interest. Congress's deliberate and narrow response in § 1346 confirms that when it wanted to extend fraud liability to intangible rights, it knew how to do so explicitly, and we should not do Congress's work for it through prosecutorial creativity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable consensus, and I find my colleagues' reasoning uniformly persuasive. Justice Kagan's observation—notable coming from a justice with different general inclinations—that the pattern of prosecutors cycling through expansive theories each time this Court narrows the statute counsels firm adherence to limiting principles is particularly compelling from an institutionalist standpoint. The strongest argument for the respondent would be that some cognizable property interest exists in the economic value of information withheld, but as Justice Barrett correctly notes, the original public meaning of 'property' at common law never encompassed a freestanding right to receive complete and accurate information bearing on economic decisions—this is not a close case on the historical record. Consistent with my institutionalist methodology, I would write narrowly to hold that 'potentially valuable economic information' bearing on 'discretionary economic decisions' does not constitute cognizable 'property' under § 1343, reaffirming the Court's consistent line from McNally through Kelly without unnecessarily reaching broader constitutional questions, thereby preserving the Court's legitimacy by demonstrating that its fraud-statute jurisprudence follows principled limits rather than prosecutorial convenience.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: My colleagues have presented a remarkably unified front, and I find the convergence of textualist, originalist, and pragmatic methodologies all pointing toward the same conclusion to be analytically significant rather than merely a product of groupthink. Justice Gorsuch's observation about Congress's targeted response in enacting § 1346 is particularly compelling from an originalist standpoint: when Congress wished to extend fraud liability to an intangible right—honest services—it did so explicitly and narrowly, which by negative implication confirms that § 1343's 'money or property' language does not silently encompass the full universe of intangible informational interests. Justice Jackson's point about fair notice and the disproportionate burden vague criminal statutes place on under-resourced defendants reinforces the constitutional dimension of this analysis beyond mere statutory interpretation. The strongest argument for the Respondent—that Carpenter v. United States recognized intangible property rights in certain contexts—is ultimately unpersuasive because Carpenter involved a recognized species of property (personal data with established legal protections), not the amorphous 'right to control' economic decisions, and McNally's limiting principle must be applied consistently regardless of how sympathetic the government's fraud theory appears in any particular case.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling—when Justices Thomas and Gorsuch reach the same destination as Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, the legal foundation is solid. Justice Kagan's pragmatic framing resonates most with my own methodology: treating the deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information' as cognizable property would effectively resurrect the intangible-rights theory McNally squarely rejected, and a pragmatic reading of the statute's text and purpose—protecting money and property, not optimizing the quality of economic decision-making—compels rejection of the right-to-control theory. My background as a public defender reinforces what Justice Sotomayor correctly identifies: an indeterminate, standardless theory of criminal liability harms vulnerable defendants most, because they cannot afford the sophisticated legal defenses needed to navigate amorphous prosecutorial theories. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be that Carpenter v. United States recognized confidential business information as property, but as Justice Kavanaugh notes, the right to receive complete and accurate information bearing on an economic decision is not a 'species of property' with roots in settled legal authority—it is a freestanding informational entitlement that would transform § 1343 into a general federal anti-deception law, precisely the boundless expansion McNally forbade.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory stretches the wire fraud statute well beyond the boundaries this Court has carefully drawn in McNally v. United States, Cleveland v. United States, and Kelly v. United States, all of which consistently hold that federal fraud statutes protect only traditional property rights, not ethereal informational interests. The research confirms that the 'right to control' theory was historically deployed as a deliberate end-run around McNally, and its revival after Skilling v. United States represents precisely the kind of prosecutorial overreach that undermines the rule of lenity and the principle that criminal statutes must provide fair notice of prohibited conduct. Consistent with my minimalist philosophy, I would resolve this case on the narrow ground that 'potentially valuable economic information' bearing on 'discretionary economic decisions' does not constitute cognizable 'property' under § 1343, without unnecessarily reaching broader constitutional questions. This narrow holding reaffirms the Court's consistent line of precedent limiting federal fraud statutes to their proper scope while preserving institutional legitimacy by avoiding the appearance that federal prosecutors may define property however expansively serves their charging decisions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1343 protects 'money or property,' and as McNally v. United States made clear, Congress enacted the federal fraud statutes to protect traditional property rights, not to create an all-purpose federal remedy for any deprivation of information bearing on economic decisions. The Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory is precisely the kind of unbounded expansion of federal fraud liability that this Court rejected in McNally, and the research confirms that the theory was consciously developed as a prosecutorial workaround to evade that decision—a history that itself reveals its illegitimacy. Under the original public meaning of 'property' at common law and at the time of the wire fraud statute's 1952 enactment, the mere deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information' necessary for 'discretionary economic decisions' was not recognized as a cognizable property interest; it is an ethereal, intangible interest untethered from any traditional property right. Cleveland v. United States and Kelly v. United States further confirm that this Court has consistently refused to permit federal prosecutors to stretch the statutory term 'property' beyond its historically grounded meaning, and fidelity to the text and original meaning of § 1343 compels the same result here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1343 protects 'money or property,' and this Court's consistent line of precedent from McNally v. United States through Kelly v. United States makes unmistakably clear that federal fraud statutes are limited to the protection of traditional property rights—not ethereal informational interests or abstract decision-making autonomy. The Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory is precisely the kind of unbounded, intangible-rights expansion that McNally rejected in 1987, and the research confirms that prosecutors have cynically revived this theory as a workaround each time this Court has constrained overbroad fraud prosecutions, including after Skilling. Treating the deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information bearing on discretionary decisions' as cognizable 'property' under § 1343 would render the statute's limiting language essentially meaningless and create a standardless federal fraud mechanism that criminalizes ordinary commercial deception far removed from any property deprivation. Principles of textualism, federalism, and fair notice all demand that we reject this theory and reaffirm that the wire fraud statute means what it says.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Despite my strong inclination to support prosecutorial tools that protect vulnerable people from fraud, the Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory stretches the wire fraud statute beyond what the statutory text and this Court's consistent precedent permit. McNally v. United States clearly limited federal fraud statutes to schemes aimed at obtaining money or property in the traditional sense, and Cleveland v. United States and Kelly v. United States have repeatedly reaffirmed that principle by rejecting expansive theories that would transform intangible informational interests into cognizable 'property.' The right-to-control theory, by treating the mere deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information' as property fraud, creates an unconstitutionally vague and boundless federal criminal statute that could sweep in enormous swaths of ordinary business conduct—a result that actually harms vulnerable defendants who face prosecution under an indeterminate standard. If Congress wishes to criminalize the deprivation of economically valuable information in decision-making contexts, it must say so explicitly, as this Court instructed in McNally and Cleveland.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory stretches the wire fraud statute well beyond what the text of 18 U.S.C. § 1343 can bear. The statute's reference to 'money or property' must be read in light of this Court's consistent line of authority—McNally, Cleveland, Kelly—holding that federal fraud statutes protect only traditional, cognizable property rights, not ethereal informational interests or the abstract right to make fully informed economic decisions. Treating the deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information' as a property interest effectively resurrects the intangible-rights theory that McNally squarely rejected in 1987, and the pattern of prosecutors cycling through expansive theories each time this Court narrows the statute counsels firm adherence to the limiting principle that Congress must speak clearly before federal criminal law expands. A pragmatic reading of the statute's text and purpose—protecting money and property, not optimizing the quality of economic decision-making—compels the conclusion that the right-to-control theory is invalid.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of 18 U.S.C. § 1343 criminalizes schemes to defraud involving 'money or property,' and as McNally v. United States made clear, this language protects traditional property rights—not ethereal informational interests like the 'right to control' one's economic decisions. The Second Circuit's theory effectively resurrects the intangible rights doctrine that McNally squarely rejected, and Congress's targeted response in enacting § 1346 to cover only 'honest services' is telling: when Congress wanted to extend fraud liability to an intangible right, it said so explicitly and narrowly. Under basic separation of powers principles, it is not the judiciary's role—and certainly not the executive branch's role through prosecutorial creativity—to expand the statute's reach beyond what Congress enacted; if Congress wishes to criminalize the deprivation of economically valuable information, it must speak clearly. The rule of lenity further compels this result, as any ambiguity about whether 'property' encompasses a victim's informational interest in making fully informed decisions must be resolved in favor of the defendant, not the government.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory stretches the wire fraud statute well beyond the boundaries this Court has repeatedly and carefully drawn. McNally v. United States established that federal fraud statutes protect property rights only, not intangible informational interests, and Cleveland v. United States reaffirmed that 'property' must be understood in its traditional sense. The right to receive 'complete and accurate information bearing on an economic decision' is precisely the kind of ethereal, non-traditional interest that Carpenter distinguished from cognizable property—it is not a 'species of property' with roots in settled legal authority, but rather an amorphous informational entitlement that would effectively transform the wire fraud statute into a general federal anti-deception law of breathtaking scope. Kelly v. United States further confirms that the object of the fraud must be traditional property, and permitting the right-to-control theory would undermine the Court's consistent institutional commitment to limiting these statutes to their proper domain, raising serious vagueness and federalism concerns that counsel strongly in favor of the petitioner.

United States, 483 U.S. 350 (1987), where the majority held that the mail fraud statute was 'limited in scope to the protection of property rights,' and which Cleveland v. United States, 531 U.S. 12 (2000), reinforced by refusing to stretch 'property' to cover interests that are not traditionally cognizable as such. Methodological consistency demands that we apply the same limiting principle uniformly: the object of the scheme must be to obtain traditionally recognized property, not merely to deprive a victim of information relevant to a discretionary economic choice.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory impermissibly stretches the wire fraud statute beyond the protection of traditional property rights, in direct tension with this Court's repeated limiting constructions in McNally v. United States, Cleveland v. United States, and Kelly v. United States. As the research materials confirm, the 'right to control' theory was historically deployed as a prosecutorial workaround after McNally rejected expansive intangible rights theories, and its revival after Skilling limited § 1346 represents precisely the kind of end-run around this Court's precedents that undermines the rule of lenity and fair notice principles I hold dear. The deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information' bearing on 'discretionary economic decisions' is not a cognizable property interest under § 1343—it is an amorphous, standardless concept that exposes an overbroad swath of conduct to federal criminal liability without the clear congressional authorization McNally demanded. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that vague, expansive theories of criminal liability fall hardest on defendants who lack resources to mount sophisticated defenses, and the Constitution requires that criminal statutes provide fair notice of what conduct is actually prohibited.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory of fraud — which criminalizes the deprivation of complete and accurate information bearing on a person's economic decision-making — constitutes a valid basis for property fraud liability under the federal wire fraud statute.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1343 (Federal Wire Fraud Statute), which prohibits the use of wire communications in furtherance of 'any scheme or artifice to defraud, or for obtaining money or property by means of false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises.'
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Ciminelli argues that the Second Circuit's 'right to control' theory impermissibly extends federal fraud law beyond its statutory boundaries by treating the deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information' necessary for 'discretionary economic decisions' as a cognizable property interest. He contends that the federal fraud statutes were designed to protect traditional, tangible property rights — not ethereal or intangible informational interests — and that expanding the statute in this manner transforms it into an all-purpose anti-corruption tool that criminalizes conduct far beyond what Congress intended, raising serious concerns about vagueness, overbreadth, and federalism.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues in opposition that the 'right to control' theory reflects a legitimate and long-standing interpretation of the wire fraud statute, maintaining that a victim's right to make informed economic decisions constitutes a cognizable property interest under federal law. The government contends that deliberately withholding material information to manipulate economic decision-making falls squarely within the statute's prohibition on schemes to defraud, and that the Second Circuit's framework appropriately captures fraudulent conduct that causes real economic harm to victims even when tangible money or property is not directly taken.
key_precedents: United States v. Binday, 804 F.3d 558 (2d Cir. 2015) — established the 'right to control' doctrine in the Second Circuit, defining the deprivation of 'potentially valuable economic information' as a property interest
McNally v. United States, 483 U.S. 350 (1987) — Supreme Court held that the mail fraud statute was limited to protection of property rights, not intangible rights such as honest government services
Cleveland v. United States, 531 U.S. 12 (2000) — Supreme Court narrowly construed 'property' under the fraud statutes, holding that state gaming licenses were not 'property' in the hands of the state
Carpenter v. United States, 484 U.S. 19 (1987) — recognized confidential business information as a form of property protected under the mail and wire fraud statutes
Skilling v. United States, 561 U.S. 358 (2010) — limited honest services fraud under 18 U.S.C. § 1346 to bribery and kickback schemes
Kelly v. United States, 590 U.S. 391 (2020) — reaffirmed that the fraud statutes require the object of the scheme to be money or property, not merely the exercise of regulatory or governmental power

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable unanimity, and I find the collective reasoning compelling and consistent with my own minimalist approach. Justice Kagan's pragmatic observation that the 'right to control' theory fails the workability test — that no limiting principle has emerged to prevent prosecutorial overreach — is particularly persuasive from an institutional legitimacy standpoint, as a doctrine without limiting principles invites the kind of ad hoc expansion that erodes public confidence in the rule of law. Justice Sotomayor's point about Congress's targeted response to McNally through § 1346 is also significant: the legislative history demonstrates that when Congress wishes to extend fraud liability to intangible interests, it acts explicitly, and courts should not preempt that judgment. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward the narrowest possible holding — that the 'right to control' theory as applied here does not satisfy the statutory requirement of cognizable 'property' under § 1343 — leaving broader questions about edge cases for another day and avoiding unnecessary constitutional pronouncements that could destabilize adjacent doctrine.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when originalists and living constitutionalists alike converge on a textual conclusion, that convergence reflects the strength of the statutory argument rather than mere ideological alignment. Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies the separation-of-powers dimension that I find most compelling: the 'right to control' theory is not merely a strained reading of 'property,' it is a deliberate prosecutorial end-run around McNally that substitutes executive creativity for congressional lawmaking, precisely the kind of interbranch usurpation that the Constitution's structural design prohibits. Justice Jackson's point about the rule of lenity and fair notice resonates with my own concern that vague criminal statutes are constitutionally suspect — the original public meaning of 'property' in 1872, when the mail fraud statute was enacted, encompassed tangible and recognized intangible property interests cognizable at common law, not an amorphous 'right to control' economic decision-making that no founding-era jurist would have recognized. Congress demonstrated in § 1346 that it knows how to extend fraud liability to intangible interests when it chooses; its silence on the 'right to control' theory is not an invitation for judicial gap-filling but a constitutional command that courts respect the boundaries of the criminal law as written.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with the conference, and Justice Thomas's originalist analysis reinforces my own textualist concerns: the phrase 'money or property' in § 1343 simply cannot be stretched to encompass a victim's abstract right to make fully informed economic decisions without doing violence to the statute's plain meaning and historical understanding. Justice Gorsuch's separation-of-powers point is particularly well-taken — the 'right to control' theory represents exactly the kind of prosecutorial bootstrapping that substitutes executive creativity for congressional lawmaking, and the historical pattern of its deployment as a post-McNally workaround is damning evidence that it lacks legitimate statutory grounding. Justice Kagan's pragmatic observation that the theory fails the workability test is also compelling from my perspective: without a coherent limiting principle, the Second Circuit's doctrine would effectively federalize every material omission in commercial transactions, creating the vagueness and overbreadth problems this Court has repeatedly sought to cabin. The strongest argument for the Respondent — that sophisticated fraudsters who cause real economic harm should not escape liability on a technicality — is ultimately a policy argument that belongs to Congress, not to courts rewriting criminal statutes.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Justice Kagan's pragmatic observation that the 'right to control' theory fails the workability test — its breadth would effectively federalize every material omission in a commercial transaction, and no limiting principle has emerged to prevent prosecutorial overreach. While I am typically more sympathetic to government prosecutions of fraud that harm vulnerable people, the absence of any coherent limiting principle here is precisely what troubles me most from a real-world impact standpoint: an overbroad statute harms not just wealthy defendants but also ordinary people who face aggressive prosecution under vague standards, as Justice Jackson rightly notes from her public defender experience. The consistent line from McNally through Kelly reflects not mere formalism but a structural commitment to ensuring that criminal liability requires fair notice and congressional authorization — values that protect the vulnerable as much as the powerful. I write separately to emphasize that my agreement with the textualist members of this Court on the outcome does not reflect endorsement of their broader methodology; rather, the convergence here reflects that even under a pragmatic, impact-focused analysis, an unbounded fraud theory creates more harm than it prevents.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of consensus, and I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum. Justice Jackson's point about the 'right to control' theory functioning as a recurring prosecutorial workaround — first after McNally, then after Skilling — is particularly compelling from a pragmatic standpoint, because it illustrates exactly the kind of institutional instability that results when courts permit elastic statutory interpretations to fill gaps Congress has deliberately left unfilled. Justice Sotomayor's observation that Congress's targeted enactment of § 1346 after McNally demonstrates the proper legislative channel for expanding fraud liability to intangible interests is the structural argument I find most persuasive: the existence of that legislative response confirms that the original statute does not reach these interests, and that any expansion requires explicit congressional action. My pragmatic textualism leads me to the same destination as my more strictly originalist colleagues here — the 'right to control' theory lacks any workable limiting principle, and without one, it would effectively federalize commercial dishonesty in ways that raise serious vagueness and federalism concerns that no amount of prosecutorial creativity can resolve.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of unanimity, and I find my colleagues' reasoning — particularly Justice Barrett's and Justice Thomas's textual and originalist analysis — entirely consonant with my own. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be that the common law of fraud historically encompassed schemes that deprived victims of economic decision-making, but that argument founders on McNally's explicit holding that the fraud statutes are 'limited in scope to the protection of property rights,' and on the structural point Justice Kagan makes well: Congress's targeted enactment of § 1346 after McNally demonstrates that expanding fraud liability to intangible interests requires affirmative legislative action, not judicial construction. The separation-of-powers concern is paramount for me — the 'right to control' theory is precisely the kind of executive-branch bootstrapping that substitutes prosecutorial creativity for congressional lawmaking, and the rule of lenity independently compels resolution of any remaining ambiguity in the defendant's favor. I write separately to emphasize that today's holding should be narrow: we reject this particular theory because it lacks any grounding in the statute's text or traditional property concepts, leaving Congress free to legislate if it concludes that informational deprivations warrant federal criminal sanction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with Chief Justice Roberts's institutionalist framing and Justice Kagan's pragmatic workability analysis — the 'right to control' theory fails both on textual grounds and as a matter of administrability, since no limiting principle has emerged to prevent it from swallowing every commercial deception involving material omissions. The convergence across our very different judicial methodologies — from Justice Thomas's originalism to Justice Jackson's rule-of-lenity and fair-notice concerns — is itself telling: when textualists, pragmatists, and institutionalists all arrive at the same destination, that consensus reflects the theory's fundamental legal infirmity rather than mere ideological alignment. From my institutionalist perspective, what troubles me most is the pattern Justice Gorsuch identifies: the 'right to control' theory was consciously developed as a prosecutorial workaround after McNally, then revived after Skilling cabined honest-services fraud, which is precisely the kind of executive branch bootstrapping that erodes the separation of powers and the Court's credibility as a consistent interpreter of statutory text. The strongest argument for the government — that real economic harm flows from information deprivation — is better addressed through congressional action, as the § 1346 precedent demonstrates, not through judicial expansion of a criminal statute that must provide fair notice to potential defendants.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with Justice Thomas's textual analysis and Justice Gorsuch's separation-of-powers framing. The historical pattern Justice Gorsuch identifies is particularly damning: the 'right to control' theory emerged as a deliberate prosecutorial workaround after McNally, was revived after Skilling cabined honest-services fraud, and represents precisely the kind of executive bootstrapping that substitutes prosecutorial creativity for congressional lawmaking. Justice Kagan's pragmatic observation that the theory fails the workability test — lacking any coherent limiting principle that would prevent federalizing every material commercial omission — reinforces my textualist conclusion that 'property' in § 1343 cannot bear the weight the Second Circuit places on it. The rule of lenity, combined with the consistent line from McNally through Kelly, compels the conclusion that where Congress has not clearly designated 'right to control economic decision-making' as protected property, courts have no warrant to supply that definition in a criminal statute.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: My colleagues have presented a remarkably unified and compelling case, and I find myself in substantial agreement with Justice Kagan's pragmatic workability analysis — the 'right to control' theory fails not only as a textual matter but as a functional one, because no limiting principle has emerged to prevent it from swallowing every material commercial omission into federal criminal liability. Justice Sotomayor's point resonates with me particularly: Congress's deliberate, targeted response to McNally by enacting § 1346 for honest services fraud is powerful structural evidence that when Congress wants to extend fraud liability to intangible interests, it knows how to do so explicitly, and courts should not substitute their own expansive constructions for that legislative judgment.
